section.title: God Renews His Promise
section.sectionRationale: God answers Moses' complaint from the end of chapter 5 with a fuller self-revelation and a sevenfold covenant promise, then the narrative pauses for a genealogy anchoring Moses and Aaron in Israel's tribal record before the confrontation with Pharaoh resumes.
section.thesis: When Moses despairs that nothing has changed, God answers not with an explanation but with Himself: I am the LORD, revealing a name Israel's fathers never fully knew and a sevenfold promise of deliverance, relationship, and inheritance.
section.frameNote: Three movements: God's promise, I am the LORD, and the sevenfold I will; Israel's unbelief from crushed spirits; the genealogy anchoring Moses and Aaron in Israel's family line.

verses.text: But the LORD said to Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh, for because of My mighty hand he will let the people go; because of My strong hand he will drive them out of his land.”
God also told Moses, “I am the {{yhwh2|LORD}}.
I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as {{elshaddai|God Almighty}}, but by My name the LORD I did not make Myself known to them.
I also established My covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan, the land where they lived as foreigners.
Furthermore, I have heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians are enslaving, and I have remembered My covenant.

Therefore tell the Israelites: ‘I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the yoke of the Egyptians and deliver you from their bondage. I will {{gaal|redeem}} you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment.
I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God, who brought you out from under the yoke of the Egyptians.
And I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I will give it to you as a possession. I am the LORD!’”
Moses relayed this message to the Israelites, but on account of their broken spirit and cruel bondage, they did not listen to him.
So the LORD said to Moses,
“Go and tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the Israelites go out of his land.”
But in the LORD's presence Moses replied, “If the Israelites will not listen to me, then why would Pharaoh listen to me, since I am unskilled in speech?”
Then the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge concerning both the Israelites and Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.
These were the heads of their fathers' houses: The sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel, were Hanoch and Pallu, Hezron and Carmi. These were the clans of Reuben.
The sons of Simeon were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. These were the clans of Simeon.
These were the names of the sons of Levi according to their records: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived 137 years.
The sons of Gershon were Libni and Shimei, by their clans.
The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lived 133 years.
The sons of Merari were Mahli and Mushi. These were the clans of the Levites according to their records.
And Amram married his father's sister Jochebed, and she bore him Aaron and Moses. Amram lived 137 years.
The sons of Izhar were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.
The sons of Uzziel were Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.
And Aaron married Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah were Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These were the clans of the Korahites.
Aaron's son Eleazar married one of the daughters of Putiel, and she bore him Phinehas. These were the heads of the Levite families by their clans.
It was this Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said, “Bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt by their divisions.”
Moses and Aaron were the ones who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt in order to bring the Israelites out of Egypt.
Now on the day that the LORD spoke to Moses in Egypt,
He said to him, “I am the LORD; tell Pharaoh king of Egypt everything I say to you.”
But in the LORD's presence Moses replied, “Since I am unskilled in speech, why would Pharaoh listen to me?”

yhwh2.gloss: The LORD, God's covenant name first disclosed fully at the burning bush. Here God repeats I am the LORD three times, bracketing the whole promise, grounding every clause of deliverance in His own unchanging being.

elshaddai.gloss: God Almighty, the name by which God revealed Himself to the patriarchs. God now says that by His name the LORD He was not fully known to them, marking a deeper stage of revelation for the generation about to be redeemed.

gaal.gloss: To redeem, the action of a kinsman redeemer who buys back a relative from slavery or debt. God casts Himself as Israel's Redeemer, the first great use of a word that will echo through the rest of Scripture, culminating in Christ's redemption of sinners.

basic.context: Moses had just complained to God that things had gotten worse, not better, since he obeyed his call. God responds not with a rebuke but with a fuller revelation of His name and a sevenfold promise: He will bring Israel out, redeem them, take them as His people, and bring them into the promised land. The chapter then pauses for a genealogy confirming Moses and Aaron's place in Israel's family tree.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a straightforward historical account of God's covenant renewal, but it is theologically dense: the sevenfold I will statements form the backbone of redemption language throughout the rest of the Bible. The genealogy, though easy to skip, roots the whole account in real, verifiable family history.
basic.originalLanguages: God says I am YHWH three times in these verses, bracketing His promise in His own unchanging name. He distinguishes this name from El Shaddai, God Almighty, known to the patriarchs. And He promises to gaal, redeem, Israel, the language of a kinsman buying back a relative from bondage.
basic.typology: God's sevenfold I will promise here, bring out, deliver, redeem, take as My people, be your God, bring in, and give as a possession, becomes the pattern of redemption fulfilled and surpassed in Christ, who redeems not from Egypt but from sin, and brings His people not into Canaan but into eternal inheritance.
basic.christ: The redemption language here, gaal, redeem, with an outstretched arm and mighty acts of judgment, anticipates the greater redemption Paul describes in Christ, who redeemed us from the curse of the law, Galatians 3:13, by His own outstretched arms on the cross.
basic.god: God is the self-revealing Redeemer who keeps every word of His covenant, even when His people are too crushed to listen. He is patient with Moses' continued reluctance, answering doubt not with rejection but with repeated reassurance grounded in His own name.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 17:1 shows God appearing to Abraham as El Shaddai. Galatians 3:13 has Christ redeeming us from the law's curse. 1 Peter 1:18-19 speaks of redemption not with silver or gold but with Christ's precious blood.
basic.oneStory: This is the theological heart of the exodus: God explains who He is and what He will do before He does it, and every clause of His sevenfold promise becomes a pattern repeated and fulfilled in the greater redemption accomplished by Christ.

context.literary:
Chapter 6 is the answer to a prayer. Exodus 5:22-23 ended with Moses asking why God had brought trouble on the people and protesting, 'You have not delivered Your people in any way.' The reply begins with 'Now you will see,' verse 1, and in verse 6 God picks up the very verb Moses used: 'I will deliver.' The complaint is not brushed aside; it is quoted back as a promise.

The speech of verses 2 to 8 is built as a frame. It opens with 'I am the LORD,' verse 2, repeats the words at its centre as the ground of the promises, verse 6, and closes with them as a final seal, 'I am the LORD!' verse 8. Inside the frame the verbs move in a line: the past (I appeared, I established My covenant), the present (I have heard, I have remembered), and then the future in a chain of first person promises that runs from Egypt to Sinai to Canaan. The whole book is sketched in advance: chapters 7 to 15 bring Israel out, chapters 19 to 40 make them God's people, and the land lies beyond the book's end.

Verses 10 to 13 and 28 to 30 form a bracket around the genealogy. Moses' objection in verse 12 is repeated almost word for word in verse 30, a device of resumption that lets the narrator step aside, list the family, and then pick up the thread exactly where he left it. The genealogy itself begins like a full list of Jacob's sons, Reuben, Simeon, Levi, but stops at the third and expands only Levi's line. That shape tells the reader what the list is for. It closes with 'It was this Aaron and Moses,' verses 26 and 27, pinning the unimpressive, hesitant speaker of verse 12 into the history of the tribe and the purpose of God. Chapter 7 then opens with God's answer to that objection.
context.historical:
The first hearers were a people who knew slavery from the inside. The word the BSB renders 'yoke' in verses 6 and 7 is the word for burdens or forced labour used in Exodus 1:11 and 2:11, the heavy loads of the brick kilns. When God says He will bring them out 'from under' those burdens, He speaks the language of their own backs.

The phrase 'outstretched arm' would also have carried weight in an Egyptian setting. Egyptian royal inscriptions and temple reliefs regularly celebrated the mighty arm of Pharaoh, and the king was pictured with his arm raised to smite his enemies. Exodus answers that boast directly: the arm that will decide Israel's future is not Pharaoh's but the LORD's, verses 1 and 6.

The genealogy reflects how Israel remembered itself, by 'fathers' houses' and clans, verse 14. The names in verses 14 to 16 match the list of those who went down to Egypt in Genesis 46:9-11, so the family that entered Egypt is the family God now claims. The ages given for Levi, Kohath and Amram, 137, 133 and 137 years, link the generations of the sojourn. Many interpreters think the list is selective, naming the key ancestors rather than every generation, since Exodus 12:40 gives the stay in Egypt as 430 years; ancient genealogies often skipped links in this way.

Several details look ahead. Amram's marriage to his father's sister, verse 20, was later forbidden in Leviticus 18:12, and the text records it without embarrassment, a sign that it predates the law. Aaron's wife Elisheba was the sister of Nahshon, verse 23, who became the leader of Judah, Numbers 1:7, and an ancestor of David, Ruth 4:20. The priestly and royal lines are joined in this one marriage.
context.canonical:
The chapter becomes the vocabulary of Israel's memory. Deuteronomy repeats the 'mighty hand and an outstretched arm' in its confessions of faith, Deuteronomy 4:34, 5:15 and 26:8, and Deuteronomy 7:8 explains why God redeemed them: 'because the LORD loved you and kept the oath He swore to your fathers.' Psalm 136:11-12 sings the same phrase with its refrain of loving devotion. Jeremiah 32:21 prays it in the dark days before the Babylonian exile, and Ezekiel 20:5-6 retells this very moment: 'I swore an oath... and made Myself known to them in the land of Egypt.'

The covenant formula of verse 7 runs like a spine through the Bible. It was first promised to Abraham, 'to be your God,' Genesis 17:7, is given here to a nation, and is repeated at the tabernacle, Exodus 29:45-46, and in the blessings of Leviticus 26:12. The prophets carry it into the new covenant, 'I will be their God, and they will be My people,' Jeremiah 31:33, a text Hebrews 8:10 quotes in full. Paul applies it to the church as God's temple, 2 Corinthians 6:16, and the final vision speaks it over the new creation, Revelation 21:3.

The 'arm of the LORD' becomes a way of speaking about the coming salvation. Isaiah 52:10 says the LORD 'has bared His holy arm in the sight of all the nations,' and Isaiah 53:1 asks, 'to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?' John 12:38 quotes that question of Jesus. Mary sings that God 'has performed mighty deeds with His arm,' Luke 1:51, and Paul in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch begins the gospel with this very moment: 'with an uplifted arm He led them out,' Acts 13:17. Later Jewish tradition tied the four cups of the Passover meal to the four verbs of verses 6 and 7, which gives added resonance to the cup Jesus took after supper, Luke 22:20.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wrote this chapter for a people who would often find, as he did, that obedience seemed to make things worse. The logic of the speech is the point. God does not give Moses a timetable or a strategy; He gives him a name and a history. Because He is the LORD, because He made a covenant with the fathers, and because He has heard the groaning, the future is settled. Israel was meant to learn that its hope rested on who God is rather than on how things looked.

The narrator is also candid about the human side. The people 'did not listen,' verse 9, not from rebellion but because their spirit was crushed, and Moses himself objects twice, verses 12 and 30. The first readers, who knew their own record of faltering, were meant to see that God's purpose was not held hostage to the faith of its instruments. He charges Moses and Aaron anyway, verse 13.

The genealogy served a practical purpose for later Israel: it located the priestly families, Aaron's sons, Korah's clan, and Phinehas, whose roles would matter greatly in Leviticus and Numbers. It told Israel that the men who led them out were real, known members of the tribe, and that the priesthood they would serve under grew from this family.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The promises of verses 6 to 8 were spoken to a particular people about a particular deliverance and a particular land, and they should not be lifted out as a guarantee that God will remove every hardship from believers today. The New Testament does not apply the land promise to Christians as real estate; it reads it through Christ and the coming inheritance.

What the chapter does model is how God meets discouragement. He answers Moses with truth about Himself, and He does not wait for Moses or Israel to feel ready before He sends them. The pattern invites believers in dark seasons to anchor themselves in God's character and promises, and it frees leaders from thinking that results depend on their eloquence. The genealogy is description, not command. Amram's marriage in verse 20, for example, is simply recorded, and it is the later law of Leviticus 18:12, not this narrative, that governs practice.

debates.question: Did the patriarchs never use or hear the name YHWH before this?

views.label: The name was unknown in its full covenant significance
views.case: Genesis uses the name repeatedly, including on God's own lips, 'I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur,' Genesis 15:7. So verse 3 is read as saying that the patriarchs knew the name but did not experience what it would come to mean. To 'be known' by a name in Hebrew idiom is to be experienced in the character the name expresses, and Exodus 6:7 says Israel will 'know that I am the LORD' by seeing the deliverance. This is the most common reading among evangelical interpreters.

views.label: The name itself was genuinely new information
views.case: Others take verse 3 at face value, that the patriarchs knew God by titles such as El Shaddai, and that the Genesis narrator used the name YHWH anachronistically, writing from Moses' perspective. Critical scholarship often used this verse as a basis for dividing Genesis into sources that do and do not use the name.

views.label: The verse is a rhetorical question
views.case: A minority reading takes the second half of verse 3 as a question: 'by My name the LORD did I not make Myself known to them?' This removes the tension with Genesis, though the Hebrew does not mark it as a question and most translations do not follow it.

debates.bearing: The first view fits the text and the rest of the Pentateuch best. The point of verse 3 is contrast in experience: the fathers received promises from God Almighty, and their children are about to see those promises kept by the LORD.

debates.question: How does a four generation genealogy fit a stay of 430 years?

views.label: The genealogy is selective
views.case: Ancient genealogies often skipped generations, naming the founders of clans rather than every link. Levi, Kohath and Amram may be clan heads, with Amram the ancestor of Moses rather than his immediate father. Numbers 3:27-28 lists the Amramites as one of four Kohathite clans numbering thousands, which is difficult if Amram were only Moses' father.

views.label: The genealogy is complete and the stay was shorter
views.case: Some take the line as complete and read Genesis 15:16, 'In the fourth generation your descendants will return here,' as confirming it. They reckon the 430 years of Exodus 12:40 from Abraham's call, including the time in Canaan, as the Greek Septuagint text of that verse does. Paul likewise counts 430 years from the promise to the law, Galatians 3:17.

debates.bearing: Either way the text's aim is not chronology but identity: to show that Moses and Aaron belong to the house of Levi and that God's word about the fourth generation is being kept. Humility is fitting where the data are compressed.

study.originalLanguages:
The title El Shaddai, 'God Almighty,' verse 3, is the name under which God gave the patriarchs promises of fruitfulness and land, Genesis 17:1, 28:3, 35:11 and 48:3. Its exact derivation is uncertain, and it is best not to build on guesses about it. What the context shows is that it was the name of promise, while YHWH here becomes the name of promise kept. The verb in 'I did not make Myself known' is a passive or reflexive form of yada, to know. Hebrew knowing is relational and experiential, not merely informational, and verse 7 uses the same verb for the goal of the exodus: 'you will know that I am the LORD your God.'

Verse 6 uses three verbs of rescue in a row. 'Bring you out,' yatsa in its causative stem, is the verb of exodus itself, and it becomes the signature of God's identity in the first commandment's preface, 'who brought you out of the land of Egypt,' Exodus 20:2. 'Deliver,' natsal, means to snatch away or rescue, and it is the verb Moses used in his complaint, 5:23, where he used an emphatic doubled form: 'You have not delivered at all.' God answers with the same verb. The third verb, gaal, redeem, comes from family law. The goel was the nearest relative who bought back a relative's land or freedom, Leviticus 25:25 and 25:48-49. By using it, God speaks of Israel as His family; He has already called Israel 'My firstborn son,' Exodus 4:22. Isaiah later joins redemption and belonging: 'I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine!' Isaiah 43:1.

'Mighty acts of judgment,' shephatim, is a plural noun that recurs in Exodus 7:4 and 12:12, where God executes judgment 'against all the gods of Egypt,' and in Numbers 33:4. The plagues are presented as a court's verdicts, not random disasters.

'I will take you as My own people,' verse 7, uses laqach, the ordinary verb to take, which is also the regular verb for taking a wife. The covenant formula that follows has the shape of a marriage declaration, and the prophets develop that picture, as in Hosea and Jeremiah 31:32.

In verse 8, 'I swore' is literally 'I lifted My hand,' the gesture of an oath. Ezekiel 20:5-6 retells this moment with the same idiom. The word for 'possession,' morashah, comes from yarash, to take possession or inherit, the verb Israel will hear constantly in Deuteronomy.

Finally, the 'broken spirit' of verse 9 is literally 'shortness of spirit,' qotser ruach, the breathlessness of people crushed by labour. And Moses' 'unskilled in speech,' verses 12 and 30, is literally 'uncircumcised of lips,' as the BSB footnote notes. The image of an uncircumcised organ, applied elsewhere to the heart, Leviticus 26:41 and Deuteronomy 10:16, means something closed or unfit for God's use. Moses is not merely claiming poor diction; he feels himself unfit to carry God's word.

typology.type: The goel, the kinsman who buys back his family, Exodus 6:6
typology.fulfillment: The kinsman redeemer had to be a near relative, able to pay, and willing to act, Leviticus 25:48-49. God casts Himself in that role for His firstborn son Israel. Christ fulfils it with a depth the law could only picture: He took on our flesh and blood to become our near kinsman, Hebrews 2:14, He was born 'under the law, to redeem those under the law,' Galatians 4:4-5, and He paid not with silver or gold but with His own blood, 1 Peter 1:18-19. The type falls short because Israel's redemption from Egypt still left the people enslaved to sin; Christ secures 'eternal redemption,' Hebrews 9:12.

typology.type: The outstretched arm that brings Israel out, Exodus 6:1 and 6:6
typology.fulfillment: The arm of the LORD stood for His power acting in history to save. Isaiah pictures that arm bared before the nations and then asks who has believed the report of it, Isaiah 52:10 and 53:1, and the arm turns out to be revealed in a Servant who suffers. John 12:38 applies that question to the unbelief that met Jesus. The escalation is striking: the decisive act of God's arm is not the drowning of an army but the Servant's own death and resurrection. Where the exodus arm struck Egypt, Christ's arms were stretched out to bear judgment Himself.

typology.type: The departure from Egypt as a pattern of salvation
typology.fulfillment: The promise to 'bring you out,' verse 6, defines the exodus, and the Gospels use that pattern for Jesus' work. On the mountain of transfiguration Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about 'His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem,' Luke 9:31; the Greek word for departure is exodos. Titus 2:14 echoes the chapter's language when it says Christ gave Himself 'to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession.' The pattern breaks where the old exodus left a generation to die in the wilderness; the new one brings every redeemed person all the way home.

typology.type: Moses the reluctant mediator with 'uncircumcised lips,' Exodus 6:12 and 6:30
typology.fulfillment: Moses stands between God and the people, carrying God's word to both, yet he feels unfit and is not heard. Hebrews 3:5-6 contrasts Moses, 'faithful as a servant in all God's house,' with Christ, 'faithful as the Son over God's house.' Jesus is the mediator whose lips were never unfit, of whom the temple officers said, 'Never has anyone spoken like this man!' John 7:46, and who could say He had made the Father's name known, John 17:26. The correspondence is real in office; the difference lies in the person, since Christ needed no Aaron to speak for Him and no reassurance to carry out His task.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ first through the name. God grounds everything in 'I am the LORD,' and the New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom that name is fully known. Jesus prays, 'I have revealed Your name to those You have given Me,' John 17:6, and 'I have made Your name known to them and will continue to make it known,' John 17:26. What the exodus generation came to know through plagues and a sea, the disciples came to know in a person. Paul says God gave the risen Jesus 'the name above all names,' so that every tongue will confess that 'Jesus Christ is Lord,' Philippians 2:9-11, language drawn from Isaiah 45:23, where the LORD alone receives that homage.

It points to Christ through the promises. Each verb of verses 6 to 8 finds its fullest meaning in Him. He has 'rescued us from the dominion of darkness,' Colossians 1:13, He delivers, He redeems, and He takes a people for Himself: 'Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God,' 1 Peter 2:10. Paul says that 'all the promises of God are "Yes" in Christ,' 2 Corinthians 1:20, and the promises of Exodus 6 are among the first and most basic of them. The new covenant He inaugurated in His blood, Luke 22:20, carries the covenant formula of verse 7 into its final form, Jeremiah 31:33 and Hebrews 8:10.

It points to Christ by contrast with Moses. Twice in this chapter Moses objects that he cannot speak and that no one will listen, verses 12 and 30. The people's spirits are too crushed to hear. Jesus meets the same deafness, John 12:37-38, yet He never falters in His charge. In Gethsemane He faced a far heavier task and prayed, 'not what I will, but what You will,' Mark 14:36. Moses was a faithful servant; Christ is the Son, Hebrews 3:5-6.

The genealogy also has a quiet Christward line. Elisheba, Aaron's wife, was the sister of Nahshon, verse 23, and Matthew's genealogy of Jesus includes 'Amminadab the father of Nahshon,' Matthew 1:4. The priestly family of Aaron and the royal line of Judah touch here. In Jesus the two offices meet in one person, a King from Judah who is also the great High Priest, Hebrews 7:14 and 8:1.

A caution belongs here. The chapter does not predict Jesus in so many words, and the genealogy should not be mined for hidden codes. The link to Christ runs through the promises God makes, through the pattern of redemption the rest of Scripture builds on them, and through the New Testament's own reading of the name, the arm, and the covenant.
study.god:
Exodus 6 teaches that God's name is His self-disclosure in action. He does not merely tell Moses what He is called; He says that by this name He will be known through what He is about to do, verses 3 and 7. God is not an idea to be defined but a person to be met in history. That is why the chapter repeats 'I am the LORD' again and again, verses 2, 6, 7, 8 and 29. Everything else He says rests on it.

The chapter shows God's faithfulness across time. He links His past acts, His present attention, and His future deeds in one sentence. 'I appeared... I established My covenant... I have heard... I have remembered... I will bring you out,' verses 3 to 6. The God who made promises to Abraham four centuries earlier has not changed or forgotten. 'Remembered' does not mean He had ever lost track; in Scripture God's remembering is His turning to act on what He has pledged, as in Genesis 8:1.

It shows the initiative of grace. In verses 6 to 8 the subject of nearly every verb is 'I.' Israel contributes nothing to the promises; they are too broken even to listen, verse 9. God's commitment does not wait for their faith. Yet the goal of the promises is relational: not only a people rescued but a people known, 'I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God,' verse 7. Deliverance is for the sake of fellowship.

It shows God as both Judge and Redeemer. The same deliverance that frees Israel comes 'with mighty acts of judgment' on Egypt, verse 6. Redemption and judgment are two sides of one act, a truth that reappears at the cross, where sin is judged and sinners are freed.

It shows God's patience with weakness. Moses objects twice with the same excuse, and God neither accepts the excuse nor rejects the man. He repeats the charge, adds Aaron, and in chapter 7 explains more. God's servants are not chosen because they are adequate; Paul later confesses that 'our competence comes from God,' 2 Corinthians 3:5.

For worship, the chapter invites believers to rest their hope on the name of God rather than on circumstances. When prayers seem to make things worse, as they did for Moses in chapter 5, God's answer is still 'I am the LORD.' Worship begins by confessing who He is, trusting what He has sworn by lifting His own hand, and waiting for Him to do what He has said.

crossReferences.note: Moses' complaint is the prompt for the whole chapter. He protests that God has 'not delivered' His people in any way, using an emphatic Hebrew form. God's answer in Exodus 6:6 takes up the same verb, 'I will deliver,' turning the charge into a promise and showing that honest lament is met, not rejected.

The covenant with Abraham already contained the two promises repeated in Exodus 6:4-8: God will be the God of Abraham's descendants, and He will give them 'all the land of Canaan' where Abraham was 'residing' as a foreigner. Exodus 6 presents the exodus as God keeping this very word.

God told Abram that his descendants would be enslaved and mistreated, that He would judge the nation they served, and that they would return 'in the fourth generation.' The genealogy's four steps from Levi to Moses, Exodus 6:16-20, and the promised judgment of Exodus 6:6 show that prophecy coming to pass.

The law of the kinsman redeemer explains the verb gaal in Exodus 6:6. An Israelite sold into slavery to a foreigner could be redeemed by a brother, uncle, cousin or close relative. God presents Himself as Israel's next of kin, the relative who pays to set His family free.

Moses later gives the motive behind the exodus promises: 'because the LORD loved you and kept the oath He swore to your fathers, He brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you.' The same hand and redemption language of Exodus 6 is traced back to God's love and oath.

Ezekiel retells the scene of Exodus 6 almost exactly: God made Himself known in Egypt, swore with an uplifted hand, and said, 'I am the LORD your God.' The prophet uses the memory to indict an exiled generation that, like the one in Egypt, failed to respond to God's self-revelation.

'To whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?' The arm that brought Israel out of Egypt, Exodus 6:6, is here revealed in the suffering Servant. John 12:38 applies the verse to Jesus, showing the exodus arm at work in His rejected ministry and death.

Paul's first recorded sermon starts with this moment: God made Israel 'a great people during their stay in Egypt, and with an uplifted arm He led them out.' He tells the exodus as the opening of a story that runs through David to Jesus, the promised Saviour.

Christ 'gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession.' Two of the Exodus 6 promises meet in one sentence, redemption and taking a people for Himself, now accomplished by Christ's self-giving rather than by plagues.

Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's new covenant, which ends with the formula of Exodus 6:7, 'I will be their God, and they will be My people.' What Sinai could not produce, a people with God's law on their hearts, Christ's covenant provides.

Peter describes redemption from 'the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers' with 'the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.' The price of redemption shifts from mighty acts against an oppressor to the costly sacrifice of the Redeemer Himself.

The voice from the throne announces: 'They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God.' The covenant relationship promised in Exodus 6:7 reaches its final form when God's dwelling is with His people in the new creation, never to be broken.

study.oneStory:
Exodus 6 stands at a hinge in the whole biblical story. Looking back, it gathers up the promises of Genesis. After the fall, God began a plan to bless all nations through Abraham's family, Genesis 12:3, and He pledged land, descendants and relationship, Genesis 17:7-8. By the opening of Exodus those promises seem stalled. The family has multiplied but is enslaved in a foreign land. Chapter 6 declares that God has not forgotten: He has heard, He has remembered, and He will act.

Looking forward, the chapter sets the agenda for the rest of the Pentateuch and beyond. God will bring Israel out, which happens in the plagues and at the sea. He will take them as His people and be their God, which is sealed at Sinai and made visible when His glory fills the tabernacle, Exodus 40:34. He will bring them into the land, which begins under Joshua. Each part is only partly realised in Israel's history. The generation that heard these words died in the wilderness, and the nation that entered the land was later driven out of it.

That failure does not cancel the promise; it deepens it. The prophets speak of a second exodus and a new covenant in which God writes His law on hearts, Jeremiah 31:33. The Gospels present Jesus as accomplishing a new exodus in Jerusalem, Luke 9:31, and shedding the blood of that new covenant, Luke 22:20. In Him God's people are redeemed from sin, not merely from a tyrant, and are made His own possession, Titus 2:14.

The story ends where the promise of verse 7 was always heading. The inheritance is not a strip of land but a renewed creation. The voice from the throne declares that God's dwelling is with humanity, 'They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God,' Revelation 21:3. The groaning heard in Egypt, Exodus 6:5, is answered by a world without tears, and the name spoken to Moses is written on the foreheads of His servants, Revelation 22:4.

sermon.title: My Name Is God Almighty
sermon.why: Piper preaches directly through Exodus 5:22-6:8, the exact hinge of this chapter, unpacking how God reminds Moses of both His name El Shaddai and His name YHWH to ground Israel's confidence in the omnipotence and covenant faithfulness of God during the darkest moment of the story.

quiz.q: How did God respond to Moses' complaint that things had gotten worse for Israel?

options.text: He revealed His name more fully and gave a sevenfold promise of deliverance, relationship, and inheritance.
options.note: Verses 2 to 8 record this direct, gracious, and detailed response to Moses' anguish.

options.text: He removed Moses from leadership.
options.note: God continues to charge Moses and Aaron with the mission in verse 13.

options.text: He remained silent and gave no answer.
options.note: God speaks at length and in detail in response to Moses' complaint.

options.text: He rebuked Moses harshly for doubting.
options.note: God's response is reassurance and promise, not rebuke.

quiz.q: What name did God say the patriarchs knew Him by, in contrast to the name LORD?

options.text: Adonai, my Lord.
options.note: This is a title of address, not the specific name the text contrasts with YHWH.

options.text: Elohim, simply God.
options.note: The text specifies El Shaddai as the contrasted name, not the general term Elohim.

options.text: El Shaddai, God Almighty.
options.note: Verse 3 states this explicitly, distinguishing the patriarchs' experience from the fuller revelation now given to Moses.

options.text: No other name is mentioned.
options.note: El Shaddai is explicitly named in verse 3.

quiz.q: Why did the Israelites not listen when Moses relayed God's promise?

options.text: Because of their broken spirit and cruel bondage.
options.note: Verse 9 gives this exact reason for their unbelief, showing suffering can deafen people even to good news.

options.text: Because they had already been freed and no longer needed the promise.
options.note: They were still enslaved; this is the opposite of their situation.

options.text: The text gives no reason for their response.
options.note: A specific reason, their broken spirit and cruel bondage, is given directly.

options.text: Because they did not trust Moses personally.
options.note: The stated cause is their crushed condition under bondage, not personal distrust of Moses.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the genealogy in the second half of this chapter?

options.text: It has no purpose in the narrative.
options.note: It serves a clear purpose, establishing Moses and Aaron's family credentials.

options.text: To record the plagues that would come.
options.note: The plagues are recorded in later chapters, not in this genealogical section.

options.text: To list the kings of Egypt.
options.note: The genealogy is entirely about Israelite family lines, not Egyptian rulers.

options.text: To anchor Moses and Aaron in Israel's verifiable tribal and family history, especially the line of Levi.
options.note: Verses 14 to 25 trace descent through Levi specifically to establish Moses and Aaron's identity and standing.

quiz.q: What Hebrew concept lies behind God's promise, I will redeem you with an outstretched arm?

options.text: Shalom, meaning peace.
options.note: Shalom is a different Hebrew concept, not the redemption term used in this promise.

options.text: Gaal, the action of a kinsman redeemer buying back a relative from bondage or debt.
options.note: This is the term used in verse 6, foundational for redemption imagery throughout Scripture.

options.text: No Hebrew concept is behind this promise.
options.note: The specific Hebrew term gaal underlies this exact promise.

options.text: Torah, meaning instruction or law.
options.note: Torah refers to teaching or law, not the redemption imagery in this verse.

questions: God answered Moses' complaint not with an explanation of the delay but with a fuller revelation of who He is. When you are struggling with unanswered questions, how might focusing on God's character rather than demanding explanations change your prayers?
The Israelites were too crushed by suffering to hear good news. Is there an area of your life where pain has made it hard for you to receive God's promises, even when they are true and near?

God's sevenfold promise moves from rescue to relationship to inheritance. Which of these, being brought out of bondage, being claimed as God's own, or receiving an inheritance, do you most need to hold onto today?
Moses still felt unqualified even after God's fresh promise, describing himself as unskilled in speech. Where do you need to trust God's commission over your own sense of inadequacy?
God is called Israel's Redeemer, One who buys back what was lost. How does knowing Christ has redeemed you at great personal cost change how you see your own worth and your own bondage to sin?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew phrase behind God Almighty is El Shaddai, whose precise etymology is debated among scholars, though its meaning of overwhelming power is well attested by its usage across Genesis and Job.
The phrase rendered broken spirit is literally shortness of spirit or breath, a Hebrew idiom for being crushed, impatient, or unable to bear more, vividly describing Israel's exhausted unbelief.
The phrase I am unskilled in speech is literally I have uncircumcised lips, a Hebrew idiom for being unfit or unable to speak effectively, repeated again by Moses in verse 30.
